HuYgTa-188510-d1e114.summary: Title line of the question for Distinction 23: whether faith is a virtue.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e123.summary: Formal statement of the question: whether faith is a virtuous habit.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e128.summary: Opening argument for the negative: no habit that was never in Christ is a virtue, since Christ, as the most perfect man, had every virtue in its highest degree. But faith was never in Christ, because faith and clear vision are incompatible, and Christ was a comprehensor from the first instant of his conception, always clearly knowing everything to be believed.
claims: Every virtue was in Christ in its highest degree.
Faith is incompatible with clear vision, which Christ had from his conception, so faith was never in Christ.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e153.summary: Argument sed contra and plan. Every intellectual habit that speaks the truth is a virtue (Ethics 6), and the faith under discussion can have no falsehood under it. The author then announces four articles: what a habit is in general; whence a habit is generated; whether we necessarily need habits and what they do for us; and the principal question.
claims: Every intellectual habit that always speaks truly is a virtue.
No falsehood can underlie the faith in question.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e177.summary: Printed summary resolution of the question: although a habit principally signifies an absolute thing, it secondarily connotes a relation. Hence a moral habit cannot be acquired by a single act in someone left to his natural course, though this can happen with intellectual habits. We need habits not in order to act at all but in order to act well.
claims: A habit principally signifies an absolute thing and connotes a relation.
A moral habit cannot be acquired by one act in someone left to the natural course, but an intellectual habit can.
Habits are needed for acting well, not for acting at all.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e197.summary: Rubric for Article 1: what a habit is in general.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e208.summary: Distinguishes three Aristotelian senses of 'habitus': (1) the disposition by which something is well or badly disposed in itself or toward another, the first species of quality; (2) the adjacency of bodies and of what surrounds them, which constitutes its own category, as in the Liber sex principiorum; (3) the abstract 'having' (habitio), a postpredicament divided into eight modes of having at the end of the Categories. The Master speaks only of the first sense, about which two conclusions are stated.
claims: 'Habitus' has three senses: a species of quality, a category of bodily adjacency, and a postpredicament of having.
The Master's discussion concerns habit as the first species of quality.
concepts: habit as first species of quality

HuYgTa-188510-d1e243.summary: First conclusion of Article 1: as to its principal signification, a habit is an absolute thing.
claims: A habit principally signifies an absolute thing.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e250.summary: Second conclusion of Article 1: by reason of what it signifies (connotes), a habit is something relative and implies a relation.
claims: A habit implies or connotes a relation.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e260.summary: First proof of the first conclusion: whatever is essentially in the category of quality is an absolute thing, at least as to its principal signification, because quality is set against relation as absolute against relative (Metaphysics 5, Categories). Habit in this sense is essentially quality, since it is the first species of quality.
claims: Whatever is essentially a quality is an absolute thing.
Habit is essentially a quality.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e283.summary: Second proof: whatever is a pure perfection, which it is better to have than not (Anselm, Monologion), is a true absolute thing, and a virtuous habit is such. Reason confirms the major: what can come to a thing without change in it is not a pure perfection, but a relation can come to its foundation without change in it.
claims: What is a perfectio simpliciter is an absolute thing.
A relation can accrue to its foundation without change in it, so it is not a pure perfection.
A virtuous habit is a perfection.
concepts: relation without change in its foundation

HuYgTa-188510-d1e310.summary: Third proof: whatever can be the principle and the terminus of created action must be absolute, since a relation can be neither (Metaphysics 5). A habit is the principle of operation, for one who has it is only in accidental potency to act and uses it at will (De anima 2), and it is the terminus of operation, since habits are generated from repeated acts (Ethics 2).
claims: A relation can be neither principle nor terminus of action or motion.
A habit is both the principle and the terminus of operation, so it is absolute.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e351.summary: Introduces three notable opinions opposed to the first conclusion. The first holds that a habit is a true relation, essentially in the category of relation; its arguments are drawn chiefly from the habit of science.
claims: One opinion holds that habit is essentially a relation.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e373.summary: First argument of the relational opinion: what is per se a species of relation is a true relation. Aristotle (Metaphysics 5) gives three modes of relation, the third being that of measure, in which the measurable is relative by its being (secundum esse) and the measure only by predication (secundum dici). Science is measured and its object is the measure, so science is relative secundum esse.
claims: In relations of the third mode the measured is relative secundum esse.
Science is measured by its object and so is a relation secundum esse.
concepts: relative secundum esse vs. secundum dici

HuYgTa-188510-d1e399.summary: Second argument: what has its principal concept in order to another principally signifies relation. Science is principally conceived in relation to the knowable, by which it is specified and distinguished; without that order it would be knowledge of nothing.
claims: Science is specified and distinguished by its knowable object.
What is principally conceived in order to another is a relation.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e424.summary: Third argument: what perishes when its correlative perishes, while all its absolute foundation remains, is essentially a relation, as paternity perishes when filiation is destroyed. Science perishes when the knowable perishes, since what is not cannot be known (Posterior Analytics 1), even though its absolute foundation remains.
claims: Relatives are posited and destroyed together.
Science perishes with the destruction of the knowable even if its foundation remains.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e454.summary: Fourth argument: a moral habit principally signifies relation, so an intellectual one does too, by parity of perfecting toward operation and toward cognition. This is proved by Augustine ('virtue is the order of love', City of God 15), since order is a relation, and by Aristotle's definition of virtue (Ethics 2), where habit is the genus and conformity to right reason, itself a relation, the formal difference.
claims: Virtue as 'ordo amoris' implies relation.
In Aristotle's definition of virtue, conformity to right reason is the formal and principal element.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e496.summary: Fifth argument: if what the intelligible generates in the intellect were absolute, so would be what the imaginable generates in the phantasy. But then several absolutes of the same species, such as likenesses of several individual men, would be in the same subject at once, which is false.
claims: Several absolute forms of one species cannot coexist in one subject.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e514.summary: Sixth argument: an absolute form perishes only by the action of a contrary, the corruption of its subject, or the corruption of a conserving principle. Science perishes without any of these: it has no contrary, the possible intellect is incorruptible, and its conserving principle can be neither the agent intellect (incorruptible) nor the act of understanding (which ceases immediately, so science would be lost at once).
claims: Science has no contrary and its subject and conserving principles are incorruptible, yet it can be lost.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e543.summary: Seventh argument: absolutes of the same proximate genus cannot coexist in the same subject, which is why two acts of understanding cannot coexist. All sciences belong to the same proximate genus, so if science were an absolute form, two sciences could not coexist in the same subject, which is false.
claims: Absolutes of the same proximate genus cannot be in the same subject at once.
Several sciences coexist in one intellect, so science is not absolute.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e565.summary: Eighth argument from Physics 7: Aristotle proves there is no motion to a habit because there is no motion to a relation. This inference holds only if habit is a relation, since a syllogism excluding a predicate through a middle term requires the middle to be affirmed of the minor; otherwise it would consist of purely negative premises. Averroes reads it as a first-figure syllogism with the minor 'every habit is toward something'.
claims: Aristotle argues there is no motion to habit because there is no motion to relation.
This argument is valid only if habit is affirmed to be a relation.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e614.summary: Ninth argument, from one proponent of this opinion: what is the intelligible species representing the object, by which the soul is in a way all things through assimilation, formally and principally implies relation, since likeness is a relation (Metaphysics 5). Science is such a species; the minor is proved next.
claims: Likeness is a relation.
Science is the intelligible species by which the soul is assimilated to its objects.
concepts: the soul is in a way all things

HuYgTa-188510-d1e641.summary: First proof of the minor of the ninth argument: the only thing we need in order to remove the absence of an object is a species representing it, and the scientific habit is such. Nothing else is needed for the act of understanding, which on some views generates science, nor to habilitate the power, since the agent and possible intellects are powers of equal abstraction, and the agent intellect needs no habilitating disposition, so neither does the possible.
claims: Only a representative species is needed to make up for the object's absence.
Since the agent intellect needs no habilitating disposition, neither does the possible intellect.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e678.summary: Second proof of the minor from Augustine: when we learn, a likeness of the thing comes to be in us (De Trinitate 9), and from the knowledge held in memory a word is begotten (De Trinitate 15), and what memory holds is a likeness. To the objection that the species precedes the act that causes the habit, the proponents reply that not every intelligible species is a scientific habit, only a species strengthened (firmata) by repeated acts.
claims: Learning produces a likeness of the thing in us.
On this view the scientific habit is an intelligible species strengthened by repeated acts.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e720.summary: Begins Thomas's replies to the relational opinion, which he rejects. To the first argument: the minor is false. Although science is a true absolute thing of the first species of quality, it necessarily involves a respect to the knowable, without which it cannot be understood, and this respect, founded on the absolute that is science, is truly in the category of relation.
claims: Science is an absolute quality that necessarily involves a relation to the knowable.
The relation is founded on science and belongs to the category of relation, but is not science itself.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e740.summary: Reply to the second argument: although science cannot be conceived without order to the knowable because of the connoted respect, that respect belongs neither to its essence nor to its principal concept. Sciences and other habits are specified and distinguished intrinsically by their own absolute entity, though extrinsically, as regards how we come to identify them, they are specified by their objects.
claims: The relation to the knowable is not of the essence or principal concept of science.
Habits are intrinsically specified by their absolute entity and only extrinsically by their objects.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e766.summary: Reply to the third argument: the minor is denied, because the absolute thing that remains when the knowable perishes is precisely what Thomas calls science.
claims: What remains when the knowable perishes is science itself.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e776.summary: Reply to the proof of the third argument's minor: what never was and never could be cannot be known, but what does not now actually exist yet once existed and remains in its likeness, the intelligible species, can well be known.
claims: What once existed and remains in an intelligible species can be known even when it no longer exists.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e798.summary: An objection to Thomas's own position: he said science necessarily involves a relation to the knowable, but now he seems to say science can remain without the knowable actually existing, and so without that relation.
claims: There appears to be a tension between saying science necessarily connotes a relation and that it can exist without its object.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e814.summary: Reply: science is not thereby freed from its respect. When the knowable is posited, science involves the relation actually; when it is removed, science still involves it aptitudinally. Similarly, a heating agent with nothing heatable still involves an aptitudinal, not actual, relation to the heatable.
claims: Science always involves its relation to the knowable, actually when the object exists and aptitudinally when it does not.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e832.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: the antecedent, that a moral habit principally signifies relation, is denied.
claims: Moral habits do not principally signify a relation.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e837.summary: Reply to the first proof of the fourth argument: Augustine's 'virtue is the order of love' is a causal, not essential, predication: virtue makes us love in an ordered way what we ought to love.
claims: 'Virtue is the order of love' is a causal predication: virtue causes ordered love.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e848.summary: Reply to the second proof: Aristotle's definition does not show that virtue is the conformity to right reason, only that it connotes such conformity to the habit of prudence, by which the virtuous person is directed in every virtuous act.
claims: Virtue connotes but is not identical with conformity to right reason.
Prudence directs every act of virtue.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e862.summary: Replies to the fifth, sixth and the beginning of the seventh arguments. Fifth: the consequent is not false, since intentional forms differing only in number can coexist in one subject; alternatively, phantasms of individuals of one species differ in species because they represent individuating accidents. Sixth: science can be corrupted by a quasi-contrary, a false-drawing (falsigraphic) syllogism opposed to the demonstrative syllogism that generates it, which can produce a false habit that leads one to set aside and forget the science. It can also be corrupted by the loss of an instrumental conserving cause, namely the long cessation of its exercise, for as we are nourished by the same things we are made of, sciences are conserved by the kinds of acts that generate them. Seventh: the major holds universally only for things of a proximate genus divided by opposed differences or contrary in some way, which is not the case for scientific habits, since science is not opposed to science, only to a falsigraphic habit. On acts of understanding, some say that they cannot coexist even though they are not opposed.
claims: Intentional forms differing only in number can coexist in one subject.
Science can be corrupted by a falsigraphic syllogism and by long cessation of its exercise.
Sciences are conserved by the same kind of acts that generate them.
Absolutes of the same proximate genus are incompatible only if they are opposed or contrary.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e949.summary: Completes the reply to the seventh argument and replies to the eighth. Acts of understanding may be incompatible because, as one bodily subject cannot actually take on several shapes at once, one spiritual subject cannot be shaped by several acts; and against the proof, the blessed simultaneously have beatific knowledge of the divine essence and natural knowledge of things in their own genus. Eighth: 'being toward something' can be understood in the first mode of per se predication (and then is essentially in the category of relation) or in the second mode (a thing of another category that receives the predication of relation). Aristotle's claim that there is no motion to relation holds in both senses: there is motion to whiteness, but not to whiteness as connoting a fitting relation to a part (as in bodily beauty). So 'every habit is toward something' is granted only in the second mode, and the syllogism concludes only that habit inseparably involves a relational property. A middle term predicated in the second mode suffices for exclusion, as in 'no risible is a stone; every man is risible; so no man is a stone'.
claims: The blessed have beatific and natural knowledge simultaneously, so different cognitions can coexist.
'Ad aliquid' can be predicated in the first or second mode of per se predication.
Habit is 'toward something' only in the second mode, so it is not essentially a relation.
A middle term predicated in the second mode of per se suffices for a valid exclusionary syllogism.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1036.summary: Possible objection: in Physics 7 Aristotle says the knower is 'most of all' said to be toward something, and Averroes says science is more worthily reckoned a relation than a quality. So science seems to be relative in the first mode, essentially, not merely by an annexed property.
claims: Aristotle and Averroes seem to place science chiefly among relatives.
concepts: the knower as most of all relative

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1059.summary: Reply: Aristotle means only that among habits it is most evident in the scientific habit that it is said 'toward something' by connoting a respect to the knowable; the temperate and the just are said toward something in the same way, but less evidently. Averroes speaks according to the opinion of others, among whom it was commonly said that science is a relation, and 'more worthily' means 'more famously'.
claims: Aristotle's remark is comparative: the relational connotation is most evident in science.
Averroes reports a common opinion rather than asserting his own.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1092.summary: Reply to the ninth argument, denying the major: as whiteness is the foundation of likeness, not formally the likeness itself, so the impressed species is the foundation of the soul's likeness to its object, not formally that likeness. The minor is also false.
claims: A species is the foundation of likeness, not formally the likeness itself.
Science is not the intelligible species.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1112.summary: Reply to the first proof of the ninth argument's minor: a habit is required to habilitate and determine the power. The parity with the agent intellect fails because the agent intellect is a natural power, acting naturally and determined to one effect, whereas the possible intellect is a rational power open to opposites and so needs a determining habit.
claims: The agent intellect, a natural power determined to one, needs no habit.
The possible intellect, a rational power open to opposites, needs a determining habit.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1137.summary: Reply to the first Augustinian authority: when we speak (or learn), a likeness of the thing arises in us because a word or definition, a perfect likeness of the thing, arises, but it does not follow that nothing else arises besides that likeness.
claims: The formation of a mental word does not exclude the generation of a habit as well.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1153.summary: Reply to the second Augustinian authority: memory holds not only intelligible species but also the scientific habit itself.
claims: Memory holds the scientific habit as well as species.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1164.summary: Rejects the proponent's reply that science is a species 'strengthened' by repeated acts. Strengthening either means only greater inherence in the subject, which is a mere respect, so that a real act would terminate immediately at a pure relation and a real relation would be newly acquired without any new absolute, both philosophically inadmissible, or it means some absolute acquired through repeated acts, which is what Thomas calls science.
claims: A real act cannot terminate immediately at a pure relation.
If strengthening adds an absolute acquired by acts, that absolute is the habit of science.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1201.summary: Second argument against the 'strengthened species' view: a thing is intensified and strengthened by the same causes that generate it, but species are not generated by acts; rather acts are generated by species (or by the object through the species). So acts do not properly strengthen a species but generate a habit really distinct from it.
claims: A thing is strengthened by the causes that generate it.
Acts arise from species, not species from acts, so acts generate a habit distinct from the species.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1217.summary: Second opinion: the habit of science is composed of an absolute as its material element and a relation as its formal element, so it is in the category of quality materially and in relation formally. Its proponents say this holds of every accident, whose material belongs to a different genus than its formal element (quantity for quality, substance for quantity), while only substance has material and formal principles in the same genus.
claims: On this view, science is materially a quality and formally a relation.
On this view, every accident's material belongs to a different genus than its form.
concepts: material and formal element of an accident

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1246.summary: Judges that the second opinion, despite its different terminology, in substance says the same as the opinion already refuted.
claims: The composition view collapses into the relational view.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1258.summary: First argument against the composition view: if 'material' means the subject, as they seem to take it, an accident is not its material but only its formal element. Whiteness is not the surface but only the quality that disperses sight. On that reading science would be only a relation, as on the first opinion.
claims: An accident is not its subject; whiteness is not the surface.
Taken this way, the composition view makes science purely a relation.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1274.summary: Second argument: the composition view speaks improperly, since an accident is not composed of its material (subject) but composed with it, a composition not 'from' these but 'to' this.
claims: An accident is composed with its subject, not out of it.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1285.summary: Third opinion: although a habit is something absolute, it is not a thing (res) but a mode of a thing.
claims: On this view, habit is an absolute mode, not a thing.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1292.summary: First argument for the modal view: what is required for a thing is a thing, but what is required only for a mode of a thing is a mode. A habit is required only for a mode of the act, namely that it be elicited promptly and with delight.
claims: A habit is required only for the manner of an act, its promptness and delight.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1310.summary: Second argument: bodily habits are modes, so the soul's habits are too. Health, a bodily habit, is not a nature but a commensuration or proportion of humors.
claims: Health is a proportion of humors and thus a mode.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1326.summary: Third argument from Metaphysics 9: immanent acts constitute nothing else, and habits are caused by repeated immanent acts, so a habit is not a constituted thing but only a mode.
claims: Immanent acts constitute nothing outside themselves.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1338.summary: Fourth argument: what is acquired by repetition and lost by mere cessation of acts is a mode, not a thing, especially in the case of acquired habits. When a horse is trained to walk, no absolute thing comes to be in it, only a customary mode, and likewise for our inclinations to good or evil from customary acts.
claims: What is gained by custom and lost by cessation is a mode.
A trained horse acquires no absolute thing, only a customary mode.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1362.summary: Rejects the modal view. First: a mode does not differ really from what it modifies, but a habit differs really from the power it perfects, since science is not the intellect.
claims: A mode does not differ really from that of which it is a mode.
A habit differs really from its power.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1373.summary: Second: if habits were modes and not things, moral science, which is entirely about habits, would be only about modes.
claims: Moral science would be a science only of modes if habits were modes.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1386.summary: Third: what per se signifies goodness per se signifies entity, since being and good are convertible. Virtuous habits per se signify goodness, since virtues are to be loved for their own sake (the Master, Book 1, d. 1).
claims: Good and being are convertible, so what is per se good is per se a being.
Virtues are to be loved for their own sake.
concepts: virtues loved for their own sake

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1405.summary: Fourth: what is a true perfection of its subject is not merely a mode, since a mode is not a perfection but results from one (as the extension of matter results from informing quantity). Virtue is a true perfection, perfecting its possessor and making his work good (Ethics 2).
claims: A mode results from a perfection but is not one.
Virtue perfects its possessor and makes his work good, so it is a perfection.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1423.summary: Fifth argument (numbered '3' in the print): what is a true species of an absolute category is not a mode distinguished from a thing, since the whole notion of the genus is included in each species. Habit is the first species of quality.
claims: A species of an absolute category cannot be a mere mode, since it includes the full notion of its genus.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1442.summary: Reply to the first modal argument: it assumes the doubtful premise that a habit contributes only to the mode of an act and not to its substance. Further, if causing a mode made something a mode, then the acts preceding the habit, which cause it, would be modes, and so would the power and object that cause acts.
claims: It is not established that habit contributes only to the mode of an act.
The modal argument proves too much: causes of modes would all be modes.
concepts: mode vs. substance of an act

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1466.summary: Reply to the second modal argument: health is not formally a proportion but an absolute quality containing and existing under such a proportion. Where philosophers say health is a commensuration of humors, the predication is causal, not formal, like Augustine's 'the soul is intellect', or it is in the second mode of per se predication.
claims: Health is an absolute quality existing under a proportion of humors.
'Health is a proportion' is a causal predication or one in the second mode of per se.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1492.summary: Reply to the third modal argument: the minor contradicts the major, since one says immanent acts constitute nothing and the other that they constitute habits. Aristotle means only that immanent acts, as immanent, constitute nothing immediately outside the agent that is not a perfection of the agent, for he himself says habits are generated from such acts (Ethics 2).
claims: Immanent acts constitute nothing outside the agent, but they do generate perfections in the agent, namely habits.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1526.summary: Reply to the fourth modal argument: the major is false, since a trained horse acquires a real quality in its joints and muscles that makes it walk better. The minor is not universally true either, since habits are usually corrupted not only by cessation of conforming acts but also by contrary acts.
claims: Training produces a real quality in the trained animal.
Habits are corrupted chiefly by contrary acts, not only by cessation.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1548.summary: States that the second conclusion of Article 1, that a habit connotes a relation, is evident from what has been said and needs no further argument.
claims: The second conclusion is evident from the preceding discussion.

HuYgTa-188510-Dd1e190.summary: Article 1, on what a habit is in general. After distinguishing three Aristotelian senses of 'habitus', Thomas takes habit as the first species of quality and concludes, first, that it principally signifies an absolute thing, because it is essentially a quality, a pure perfection, and the principle and terminus of action, none of which a relation can be. Second, it connotes a relation. He refutes three opinions. Against the view that habit (especially science) is essentially a relation, he holds that science is an absolute quality founding a respect to the knowable, intrinsically specified by its own entity, related actually or aptitudinally to its object, and corrupted by falsigraphic reasoning or disuse. He reads Aristotle's 'no motion to a habit' through the second mode of per se predication, and he rejects the claim that science is a species 'strengthened' by acts. The composition view (absolute matter plus relational form) collapses into the first. The modal view (habit as an absolute mode, not a thing) fails because habits differ really from powers, are per se good and true perfections, and are species of quality; a trained horse acquires a real quality.
claims: A habit principally signifies an absolute quality and connotes a relation.
Science is an absolute quality founding a relation to the knowable; it is not itself a relation.
Habits are specified intrinsically by their own entity, extrinsically by their objects.
A habit is a real thing, not a mere mode, because it differs really from its power and is a true perfection.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1555.summary: Rubric for Article 2: whence a habit is generated or proceeds.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1565.summary: Opens Article 2 with a parallel between theories of the generation of natural forms and of habits. On natural forms: Anaxagoras's latency of forms (entirely from within), Avicenna's giver of forms (entirely from without), and Aristotle's middle position (partly from the potency of matter, partly from the agent). On habits: Plato's innate, concreated sciences and virtues, so that learning is reminiscence; Avicenna's derivation from the separate intelligence; and Aristotle's view that habits are in us by nature in aptitude but are perfected in act by exercise, since like acts generate habits (Ethics 2). Experience confirms that repeated acts produce inclinations toward similar acts. The disputed point is whether a habit is generated by one act or requires many, on which two conclusions follow.
claims: Aristotle's middle position is correct: habits are naturally in us in aptitude and acquired in act by exercise.
Repeated acts generate inclinations to similar acts, which are habits.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1638.summary: First conclusion of Article 2: in a human being left to the natural course, the first moral virtue cannot be acquired by a single act.
claims: The first moral virtue cannot be acquired by one act in someone left to the natural course.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1647.summary: First proof: when a subject has dispositions opposed to the form to be introduced, these must first be weakened, since agents act only on a disposed patient (De anima 2). Because of original sin, human beings are disposed against moral virtue, for 'the senses and thoughts of the human heart are prone to evil from youth' (Genesis 8).
claims: Opposed dispositions must be removed before a form is introduced.
Because of original sin, humans are disposed against moral virtue.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1669.summary: Second proof: from infancy people become accustomed to sensible goods and contract a difficulty toward moral virtue; this softness, not easily removed, must be overcome by repeated acts before virtue is acquired. Thomas stresses 'first' virtue: once one virtue is perfectly acquired, either all moral virtues are present with it because of their connection, or at least any other can be introduced by a single act, since the subject is no longer contrarily disposed.
claims: Habituation to sensible goods creates a resistance to virtue that only repeated acts remove.
Once one virtue is perfectly acquired, the others are present or can be acquired by one act, because of the connection of the virtues.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1704.summary: An opposing view of a certain doctor: the first act introduces the whole essence of the habit and later acts increase and perfect it. Later acts either increase what the first made, or make something of another species (impossible, since they are of the same kind), or something numerically distinct (impossible, since two accidents differing only in number would be in one subject).
claims: On this view, the first act introduces the whole essence of a habit.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1730.summary: Reply: the first act does something, but not the essence of the habit; it weakens or destroys the dispositions opposed to the habit to be introduced, as fire's first action on something cold does not at once produce heat but reduces the cold.
claims: The first act removes contrary dispositions rather than producing the habit's essence.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1749.summary: Second conclusion of Article 2: in intellectual habits, especially speculative ones, the whole habit can be introduced by one act, meaning a complex act of reason in which a whole demonstration counts as one act. For conclusions immediately grounded in first principles the intellect is already sufficiently disposed, and a plurality of preceding acts is needed in introducing forms only to dispose the subject.
claims: A speculative intellectual habit can be generated by a single demonstrative act.
Many acts are needed only where the subject must first be disposed.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1784.summary: Objection to the supposition of both conclusions: a habit is nobler than the acts preceding it, since it makes later acts more perfect, and an effect is never nobler than its cause, whether equivocal or univocal. So habits cannot be caused by acts.
claims: An effect cannot be nobler than its cause.
A habit is nobler than the acts preceding it.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1810.summary: Reply: something less noble can cause something nobler by another's power, not its own. The acts preceding a habit cause it by the power of the possible intellect that elicits them, of the will whose intention joins offspring to parent and continues the acts, and of the agent intellect that illuminates the intelligible species, without which the possible intellect could neither receive species nor understand.
claims: A less noble cause can produce a nobler effect by a higher power.
Acts generate habits by the power of the possible intellect, the will, and the agent intellect.

HuYgTa-188510-Dd1e1552.summary: Article 2, on the origin of habits. Paralleling theories of natural forms (Anaxagoras, Avicenna, Aristotle), Thomas sides with Aristotle against Platonic innatism and Avicenna's separate giver: habits are in us by nature in aptitude and acquired in act through exercise. He then argues that in someone left to the natural course the first moral virtue cannot be acquired by one act, because original sin and habituation to sensible goods create contrary dispositions that only repeated acts remove. Once one virtue is acquired, the others follow at once or by single acts because of their connection. Against a doctor who holds that the first act produces the whole essence of a habit, he says the first act only weakens contrary dispositions. Speculative intellectual habits, however, can be produced by a single demonstrative act. The objection that a habit is nobler than its causing acts is met by saying the acts work by the power of the possible intellect, the will and the agent intellect.
claims: Habits are naturally in us in aptitude and acquired in act by exercise.
The first moral virtue cannot be acquired by one act, because of contrary dispositions from original sin and custom.
A speculative intellectual habit can be produced by a single demonstration.
Acts generate a nobler habit by the power of higher principles.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1836.summary: Rubric for Article 3: whether we necessarily need habits and what habits do for us.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1849.summary: First conclusion of Article 3: although we do not need habits to act in any way at all, we do need them to act well (the printed 'vt agamus' evidently means 'to act well', as the summary resolution states).
claims: Habits are not needed for acting simpliciter but are needed for acting well.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1860.summary: First proof: for an act to be elicited well and easily it must be elicited with delight, and delight in the work is the sign of a generated habit (Ethics 2).
claims: Pleasure in acting is the sign of a habit.
Good and easy action requires delight, hence a habit.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1872.summary: Second proof: whatever can err needs something to keep it in rectitude. Rational powers, being open to opposites, can err in determining themselves, so by reason of their freedom and indeterminacy they need virtuous habits to determine them to the good and preserve them from error.
claims: Rational powers, being free and indeterminate, need habits to determine them to the good.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1890.summary: Third proof: as acting presupposes being, acting well presupposes being well. Being good cannot be continued in us by acts, since we cannot always be acting (De somno et vigilia), so it must be continued by a virtuous habit.
claims: Good acting presupposes good being.
Since acts are intermittent, goodness must be sustained by a habit.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1910.summary: Fourth proof: we need for good action that by which we are well disposed toward ourselves and others, and that is a virtuous habit, per the Metaphysics 5 definition of habit as what disposes well or badly.
claims: Habit, by definition, disposes us well or badly toward ourselves and others.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1923.summary: An objection: if we need habits, it is either for the substance of the act or for its mode. Not for the substance, since a bare power can produce its act, as experience shows. Not for the mode either, since on Thomas's view a mode does not differ from what it modifies, so what does not contribute to the substance does not contribute to the mode. Confirmation: rational powers are more perfect than natural powers, which need no habits for substance or mode.
claims: A bare power can produce the substance of its act.
If mode and act are identical, what does not contribute to one does not contribute to the other.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e1967.summary: Second conclusion of Article 3, resolving the objection: a habit contributes neither precisely to the substance of the act nor precisely to its mode, but to the modified substance of the act. Not precisely to the substance, since then it would cooperate with the power in nothing, as the bare power suffices for the bare act. Not precisely to the mode, since what cannot be separated from something cannot have a separate cause, and the mode of a perfect act is really identical with the act.
claims: A habit causes the modified act, not merely its substance or merely its mode.
The mode of a perfect act is really identical with it and cannot have a cause distinct from the act's cause.
concepts: substance vs. mode of an act

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2011.summary: First proof that a habit causes the modified act: what enables a power to produce a modified act is a cause of that act, and the habit is such.
claims: The habit enables the power to produce the modified act and is therefore its cause.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2023.summary: Second proof: an effect with a simple entity that depends on two things as one perfect principle must be reduced to each of them in its whole entity. The modified act from a power perfected by a habit is simple, as the whiteness of a pearl is no less simple than that of a wall though more beautiful, and it depends on power and habit as on one perfect principle. This is shown by God, whose knowing is most perfect though his knowledge is really identical with his intellective power.
claims: An act's perfection does not detract from its simplicity.
Power and habit act as one complete principle of the perfect act.
In God, knowledge and intellect are identical and yet his knowing is most perfect.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2071.summary: Opposing opinion of certain doctors: the power alone causes the act as to its essence, and the habit only as to its mode.
claims: On this view, the power causes the act's essence and the habit only its mode.
concepts: essence vs. mode of an act

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2082.summary: First argument for the opposing opinion: every power can produce its proportioned act without anything added as the reason for eliciting it, and understanding is proportioned to the intellect, desiring to the appetite, and so on.
claims: A power can produce its proportioned act without any addition.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2095.summary: Second argument: as supernatural power relates to supernatural habit, so natural power relates to naturally acquired habit. The supernatural power of consecrating causes the essence of the act of consecration, while charity contributes only its mode, namely that it be performed meritoriously.
claims: In consecration, the priestly power causes the act and charity only its meritorious mode.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2121.summary: Third argument from Ethics 2: a power is that by which we can, a habit that by which we can well or badly. What causes the essence of an act is that by which we 'can', so if a habit caused the essence of the act it would be a power.
claims: Power is that by which we can; habit that by which we can well or ill.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2140.summary: Fourth argument: a habit is the principle of that for which we need it, and we need it only for the mode.
claims: We need habits only for the mode of acting.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2154.summary: Refutation of the opposing opinion: whenever one thing relates to another as first act to second act, it causes the second even as to its essence. A habit relates to operation as first act to second (De anima 2, science and considering), at least as compared to the perfect act.
claims: First act causes second act even as to its essence.
Habit is first act relative to operation.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2181.summary: Reply to the first argument: a bare, imperfect act is proportioned to the power by itself, but a perfect act is proportioned only to a power perfected by a habit.
claims: Only a habit-perfected power is proportioned to a perfect act.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2194.summary: Reply to the second argument: the analogy fails, since charity is not a habit proper to consecration but a common form for every good work, proper only to the act of loving, while acquired habits are determinate virtues for determinate acts. One might also say that the power of consecrating is in God, not in the priest, so created charity is not the form of the principal power eliciting consecration and need not reach its essence. Acquired habits, by contrast, perfect the very powers that elicit their acts and so, together with them, cause those acts even in their essence.
claims: Charity is a general form of good works, proper only to the act of love.
The power of consecrating is principally in God, not in the priest.
Acquired habits, as perfections of their powers, cause their acts even in essence.
concepts: charity as form of the virtues

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2238.summary: Reply to the third argument: Aristotle speaks by appropriation. Substance, act and mode are really the same, so both the perfected power and the perfecting habit cause the whole modified act; but the act is appropriated to the power as to substance and to the habit as to mode, for two reasons. First, when an indeterminate and a determining principle concur, our way of understanding attributes the essence to the indeterminate one and the mode, a sort of determination, to the determining one; powers are indifferent to virtuous and vicious acts and are determined by habits. Second, when one concurring principle presupposes the other, the essence is attributed to the presupposed and the mode to the presupposing, since conceptually a mode presupposes an essence; the habit presupposes the power.
claims: Both power and habit cause the whole modified act.
The essence is appropriated to the power and the mode to the habit only according to our way of understanding.
Powers are indifferent to virtue and vice and are determined by habits.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2301.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: we do not need a habit to elicit an imperfect act, but to elicit a perfect act we need it not only for the mode but also for the essence, since mode and essence are not separable there, being really the same.
claims: For a perfect act a habit is needed for essence as well as mode.

HuYgTa-188510-Dd1e1839.summary: Article 3, on whether and why we need habits. Thomas holds, first, that we need habits not for acting at all but for acting well: good action requires delight, the sign of habit; rational powers open to opposites need determination; good being must be sustained between intermittent acts; and habit is what disposes us well. Second, against the dilemma of whether habits serve the substance or the mode of an act, he holds that habit causes the modified act as a whole, since the mode of a perfect act is really identical with it. Power and habit act as one perfect principle of a simple act, as in God, whose knowledge is his intellect. He rejects the view that the power causes the essence and the habit only the mode: habit is first act relative to operation; the consecration-charity analogy fails because charity is a general form and the power of consecration belongs principally to God; and Aristotle's assignment of 'can' to power and 'can well' to habit is only an appropriation according to our way of understanding.
claims: Habits are necessary for acting well, not for acting simpliciter.
A habit causes the modified act as a whole, not merely its mode.
Power and habit together constitute one perfect principle of a perfect act.
Attributing essence to power and mode to habit is only an appropriation.
concepts: substance vs. mode of an act

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2319.summary: Rubric for Article 4: whether faith is a virtue.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2331.summary: Opens Article 4 by distinguishing two kinds of faith. Acquired faith need not be a virtue and may even be a vicious habit, since some acquire erroneous faith opposed to Catholic truth. Two conclusions are then stated about faith infused by God.
claims: Acquired faith need not be virtuous and can be vicious.
The question properly concerns infused faith.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2357.summary: First conclusion: taking virtue as any praiseworthy habit inclining a power to praiseworthy and meritorious acts, infused faith is a virtue. God infuses faith so that we may assent to supernatural truth, an assent necessary for eternal salvation, praiseworthy in itself and meritorious when charity is present.
claims: Infused faith is a virtue in the broad sense of a praiseworthy habit.
Assent to supernatural truth is necessary for salvation and meritorious with charity.

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2379.summary: Second conclusion: taking virtue in the Philosopher's usual sense, as the ultimate of a power, the habit that brings a power to the highest perfection its act can reach, faith is not a virtue. The intellect attains the object of faith more perfectly through the light of glory, wholly clearly, than through the light of faith, which is enigmatic.
claims: In the Aristotelian sense of 'ultimum de potentia', faith is not a virtue.
The light of glory attains faith's object more perfectly than the enigmatic light of faith.
concepts: virtue as the ultimate of a power

HuYgTa-188510-d1e2403.summary: Reply to the opening argument by referring to the Prologue of Book 1 (q. 5, a. 2), where Thomas showed how clear vision is compatible with faith and how it conflicts with it: as a habit, faith has no incompatibility with clear vision.
claims: As a habit, faith is not incompatible with clear vision, so it could exist in Christ.

HuYgTa-188510-Dd1e2326.summary: Article 4 answers the principal question. Acquired faith need not be a virtue and may be vicious when erroneous. Infused faith is a virtue if virtue means any praiseworthy habit inclining to praiseworthy and meritorious acts, since it enables the assent to supernatural truth needed for salvation. It is not a virtue in Aristotle's strict sense of the habit that brings a power to its ultimate perfection, since the light of glory attains the same object more perfectly than the enigmatic light of faith. The opening argument that faith was not in Christ is answered by appeal to the Book 1 Prologue: as a habit, faith is compatible with clear vision.
claims: Acquired faith can be vicious.
Infused faith is a virtue in the broad sense of a praiseworthy, meritorious habit.
Infused faith is not a virtue in the strict sense of 'ultimum de potentia'.
The habit of faith is compatible with clear vision.
concepts: light of faith vs. light of glory

HuYgTa-188510.summary: Quaestio 1 on Distinction 23: 'Whether faith is a virtue'. Before answering, Thomas builds a general theory of habit in three articles. (1) A habit, as the first species of quality, is principally an absolute thing that connotes a relation; he refutes the views that it is essentially a relation (with extended discussion of science, its relation to the knowable, its corruption and its distinction from the intelligible species), a compound of absolute and relation, or a mere mode. (2) Following Aristotle against Plato and Avicenna, habits are innate in aptitude and acquired by exercise; the first moral virtue needs many acts because of contrary dispositions from original sin and custom, whereas a speculative habit can come from one demonstration. (3) Habits are needed not for acting but for acting well, and they cause the modified act as a whole, together with the power as one principle. (4) Acquired faith may be vicious, but infused faith is a virtue in the broad sense of a praiseworthy habit ordered to meritorious assent, though not in Aristotle's strict sense, since the light of glory surpasses it. The objection that Christ lacked faith is answered by the compatibility of the habit of faith with clear vision.
claims: A habit is principally an absolute quality that connotes a relation.
Moral virtue is not acquired by a single act, but a speculative intellectual habit can be.
Habits are needed to act well and cause the modified act together with the power.
Infused faith is a virtue in the broad sense but not in the strict Aristotelian sense.
The habit of faith is compatible with clear vision.
